title: Benetton postponement: dye per-tenant fine-tunes at compute time
idea: Benetton knits undyed sweaters and dyes them at the last moment. One base model stays resident and serves thousands of fine-tuned variants. Each variant is stored as a 1-bit sign delta plus per-row scales (or a low-rank adapter), and the 'dye' is fused into the GEMM, so no variant is ever materialized in DRAM.
why: N full model copies become one base plus N deltas of about 1/16 the size, a 10-100x memory reduction for multi-tenant fine-tune hosting.
note: BitDelta and S-LoRA/Punica are prior art.

title: Swap fp32 vector-index embeddings for 1-bit codes plus SSD rerank
idea: Substitute full-precision vectors in DRAM with sign-bit codes. Vector databases keep only binary codes in DRAM for Hamming-distance candidate search (popcount on existing CPUs) and read the fp32 vectors of the top ~100 candidates from NVMe to rerank.
why: Billion-vector RAG and search indexes shrink ~25x in DRAM at about a 1-point recall loss, with unchanged DDR.
note: Binary codes plus rerank already standard in vector DBs.

title: Minify vector-DB residency to 1-bit codes plus flash rerank
idea: Minify every resident embedding to a binary sign code (32x smaller than FP32). Candidates are found by popcount Hamming search in DRAM and reranked with full-precision vectors fetched from NVMe.
why: Vector databases hold 32x more vectors per GB of DRAM at near-equal recall.

title: Bit-plane segmented KV cache with attention-gated plane residency
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation: split every FP16 KV vector into a high plane (sign, exponent, top mantissa bits) and a low-mantissa plane stored in separate pages; only high planes stay in HBM, low planes live in CXL/LPDDR or NVMe and are fetched only for tokens whose coarse attention score (computed from high planes alone) lands in the top-k. Resolves 'keep all context' vs 'keep little memory' by holding every token coarsely and few tokens fully, losslessly.
why: KV cache dominates long-context serving memory; ~2-3x less HBM per session with a lossless fallback, so fewer HBM stacks (HBM TSV tax, cost/bit).
note: Coarse high planes for scoring plus lossless low-plane fetch for top-k; limited to ~2x.

title: Bicycle gears: bit-plane tiering serves weights at shiftable precision
idea: Store weights transposed into bit-planes: the 4 most-significant planes stay in DRAM/HBM, low planes live in CXL or flash; each request 'shifts gear' by fetching only as many planes as its quality tier needs, and speculative decoding uses MSB-only planes as a free draft model.
why: Cuts DRAM held for weights 2-4x without storing multiple quantized copies; fetch energy scales with precision actually used.

title: Molybdenite exfoliation: peel only the bit-planes a token needs
idea: MoS2 peels into single layers; weights are stored bit-plane-major in row-aligned tiles (all MSBs of a tile together, then the next bit), and a per-token difficulty predictor fetches 2, 3, 4 or 8 planes, so easy tokens run a lower-precision model from the same single copy without overfetching unused planes.
why: Fetching 2-3 planes for most decode steps instead of 16-bit weights cuts weight bits moved ~6-8x on average and >10x on easy tokens, and LSB planes of cold layers can be evicted to flash (energy, density).

title: Client-parked compressed KV state between conversation turns
idea: After each turn, the server sends the user's device or the nearest edge PoP a compressed, encrypted latent state of ~0.5-2 MB (MLA-style low-rank KV or a distilled gist-token set). The next request uploads it back. The datacenter then holds no per-session state across gaps of minutes to days.
why: The long-timescale residency of KV moves off scarce HBM/DRAM onto idle client storage. Datacenter session memory shrinks toward only the active-decode set.
note: Offloading session state to clients is fresh; long-context KV exceeds 2 MB unless lossy gist compression holds quality.

title: Hashed compositional embeddings plus a learned head cache
idea: Combine the hashing trick (each ID composes its vector from several shared sub-tables via independent hashes) with a small table of fully learned rows for the hottest IDs; IDs are promoted to full rows as their frequency rises and demoted when they cool.
why: Recommendation models hold multi-TB embedding tables in DRAM; the long tail compresses 10-50x with little accuracy loss.
note: QR/hashing-trick embeddings with frequency-based promotion are known.

title: Garbage collector fused with a columnar compressor for old generation
idea: Combine the generational GC's copying/promotion phase with compression: objects promoted to the old generation are packed into per-class columnar blocks (field-transposed, delta- and dictionary-encoded), and a read barrier decompresses on access through a small decoded-object cache.
why: Managed heaps (Java, Go, JS, Python) run at 2-5x live data with highly redundant fields; a 2-3x old-gen shrink is plausible.

title: Vacuum pack with crash foam: compress pages, fill freed space with ECC
idea: Packers shrink-wrap a product and fill the leftover box space with foam. Each 4 KB page in the compressed tier is compressed, and the freed bytes hold a long LDPC/BCH code sized to the space left over. At page scale, 1% raw BER needs about 15-23% parity, so any page that compresses 1.3x or better carries its own armor at no capacity cost. Incompressible pages go to a small protected tier.
why: Flaky 1%-BER cells deliver DRAM-grade reliability for the roughly 70% of pages that compress, with net capacity still about 1.6x thanks to the compression.

title: One latent per token regenerates every layer's K/V on demand
idea: Inverts 'each layer stores its own KV cache': DRAM holds a single low-rank latent per token (e.g., 256 dims), and each layer's tensor cores up-project it to K and V just in time inside the attention kernel, spending cheap FLOPs to save scarce bytes. A short distillation pass retrofits existing models so the shared cross-layer latent is trained jointly.
why: KV-cache bytes drop 10-40x vs per-layer FP16 KV, beyond per-layer latent attention, so long-context serving fits in a fraction of the HBM/DRAM.
note: 10-40x KV cut if one latent serves all layers; doubt: retrofit by short distillation; MLA/CLA partly there.

title: IBM MXT, fixed: compression moved behind CXL where latency is free
idea: MXT (2000) compressed all memory in 1 KB sectors behind a 32 MB L3, so every miss paid decompression and the extra cache chip cost more than the DRAM saved. Put an LZ4/zstd engine inside a CXL Type-3 expander that already costs ~150-250 ns, compress at 4 KB with a 64 MB uncompressed hot-line buffer, and expose 2-3x physical capacity as plain memory.
why: Cost per bit: 2-3x effective GB in the far tier; decompression hides inside the existing CXL hop, removing the latency and cost penalty that killed MXT.
